As for your question, humans have been aware of the existence of outer space for thousands of years. The earliest recorded observations of the night sky date back to ancient civilizations in Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Greece. These cultures recognized the stars and constellations, and some even believed that the stars were gods or spirits.

The ancient Greeks, in particular, were known for their sophisticated understanding of the universe. They believed that the stars and planets were made of a material called "aether," which was thought to be a divine substance. The Greek philosopher Aristotle (384-322 BCE) also wrote extensively on the nature of the universe, including the concept of the "void" or empty space between the stars.

However, it wasn't until the 16th century that the modern understanding of outer space began to take shape. The Polish astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus (1473-1543 CE) proposed the heliocentric model of the universe, which placed the Sun at the center of the solar system. This idea was later supported by the work of Galileo Galilei (1564-1642 CE) and Johannes Kepler (1571-1630 CE), who discovered the laws of planetary motion.

The first telescopes were developed in the 17th century, allowing astronomers to study the night sky in greater detail. The discovery of the first galaxies, such as Andromeda, in the 18th century further expanded our understanding of the universe.

As for the color of space, it's actually a bit more complicated than a simple blue. The color of space is often described as black, because it absorbs all wavelengths of visible light. However, when we look at the stars and galaxies, we see a range of colors, from red to blue to white. This is because the light from these objects is scattered and absorbed by the interstellar medium, which is the material that fills the space between the stars.

In the early days of space exploration, astronauts did indeed see the Earth as a blue planet, but this was due to the way that the atmosphere scatters sunlight. The blue color of the Earth is caused by the scattering of shorter wavelengths of light, such as blue and violet, by the atmosphere. This is why the Earth appears blue from space, but not because the space itself is blue.
